analysis.one_liner: Makes workers' pension shortfalls a top-priority claim when their employer goes bankrupt.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was introduced in October 2017 with 8 Democratic cosponsors, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and died there when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company with a traditional pension plan goes bankrupt, workers can end up last in line for the money they were promised. This bill would change the bankruptcy code so that the unfunded part of a company's pension promises, and the pension withdrawal charges the law already imposes on companies leaving shared pension plans, count as top-priority debts that must be paid ahead of banks and other creditors. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees covered by traditional defined-benefit pensions, especially multiemployer union plans, whose benefits would be paid ahead of corporate lenders if their employer entered bankruptcy.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the bankruptcy code so that all unfunded vested benefits in a defined-benefit pension plan count as allowable administrative expenses, which receive first priority in bankruptcy proceedings [S2].
Gives the same top priority to withdrawal liability owed under ERISA when an employer exits a multiemployer pension plan [S2][S3].
Conforms section 507(a)(5), the bankruptcy priority list, so the new pension claims rank ahead of the general creditor claims that currently sit at that level [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, bondholders, and other corporate creditors, who would be paid after pension shortfalls instead of ahead of them, and companies with large pension obligations, whose bankruptcy debts would grow.

drawbacks.text: Moving pension shortfalls ahead of secured and ordinary creditors changes the expected recovery in every bankruptcy involving a pension plan; lenders could respond by charging higher rates or demanding stronger collateral from companies with large pension obligations, raising their cost of credit [S3].
The bill addresses only the ranking of claims in bankruptcy. It does not shore up the pension insurance system itself or the pension funds of companies that never reach bankruptcy court [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers covered by traditional pensions, the change is straightforward: money they were promised moves ahead of money owed to lenders, and a federal insurance backstop (the PBGC) has to cover less. The cost is a reordering of bankruptcy risk that lands on corporate creditors, who would likely price that risk into loans to pension-heavy companies. The bill does nothing for pensions outside bankruptcy, so it is a targeted fix, not a broad one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no further action ever was taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Ryan introduced the bill on October 5, 2017, joined by Rep. Donald Norcross [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On October 16, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where the action history ends [S5].
It drew 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee vote or floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate lenders and creditors kept their current place ahead of workers' pension claims in bankruptcy, and pension-heavy companies avoided a larger debt burden in bankruptcy. Workers whose pensions depend on how a bankruptcy unfolds got no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate creditors kept their priority over pensions

for.name: Rep. Tim Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give pension shortfalls top-priority status in bankruptcy.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Joined Rep. Ryan in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; never held a markup or sent it to the floor.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Their promised benefits would rank ahead of corporate lenders in a member-employer's bankruptcy, recovering more money for retirees directly.
Pension shortfalls would be paid ahead of their claims, cutting their recoveries in bankruptcies of pension-heavy companies. Their gain under the status quo is workers' loss.
Their bankruptcy debts would grow, but they would face less pressure from the federal pension insurer stepping in when they fail.
